p.src: Our tale tells how the Tang Monk and his disciples used their magic powers to hold back the monks of the Cloth-of-Gold Monastery. When the monks saw that master and disciples had vanished wherever the black wind passed, they took them for living Buddhas descended to the mortal world, kowtowed, and returned; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: There is no telling all their morning meals and evening lodgings, their crossings of ravines and searches for streams. They travelled for half a month along that peaceful road. Ahead of them they once again saw the walls of a city drawing near. Tripitaka asked, “Disciples, what place is this now?” The Pilgrim replied, “I don't know, I don't know.” Eight Rules laughed and said, “You have travelled this road before, so how can you say you don't know? There must be some trick here. You're deliberately pretending not to recognize it just to make fools of us.” The Pilgrim said, “This idiot understands nothing of the matter. Though I have passed along this route several times, I was then high in the ninth heaven, coming and going upon the clouds. When did I ever set foot in this place? Since it was no concern of mine, why would I investigate it? That is why I do not know. What trick could there be, and how am I making a fool of you?”

p.src: As they spoke, they arrived at the city before they knew it. Tripitaka dismounted, crossed the drawbridge, and went straight through the gate onto the main street, where he saw two old men sitting beneath a covered walkway in conversation. Tripitaka called out, “Disciples, stand there in the middle of the street, keep your heads lowered, and do not behave wantonly. Wait while I go beneath the walkway and ask what place this is.” The Pilgrim and the others obediently stood still. The elder approached with palms joined and called, “Good aged patrons, this poor monk offers you greetings.” The two old men had been idly discoursing upon rise and decline, gain and loss, who was a sage and who a worthy, and where the heroic achievements of former days could now be found—a subject truly fit for deep lamentation. Suddenly hearing his greeting, they returned it and asked, “What would you say to us, elder?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk has come from afar to pay homage to the Buddha. I have only just reached your honoured region and do not know the name of this place. Where might there be a virtuous household from which we could beg a vegetarian meal?” An old man replied, “Our humble locality is Copper Terrace Prefecture. Beyond the prefectural city lies a county called Earth-Spirit County. If you want a vegetarian meal, elder, there is no need to beg. Pass this memorial arch and go to the north-south street. On its western side, facing east, stands a gatehouse with a crouching tiger. It belongs to Squire Kou, and before his gate is a tablet inscribed ‘No Monk Among Ten Thousand Shall Be Turned Away.’ A monk from afar such as you may enjoy his hospitality to the full. Go! Go! Go! Do not interrupt our conversation.” Tripitaka thanked them. Turning back, he said to the Pilgrim, “This place is Earth-Spirit County in Copper Terrace Prefecture. Those two old men said, ‘Beyond this memorial arch, on the north-south street, there is an east-facing gatehouse with a crouching tiger. It belongs to Squire Kou, and before his gate is a tablet reading “No Monk Among Ten Thousand Shall Be Turned Away.”’ They told me to go to his house for a vegetarian meal.” Sha Monk said, “The Western Region is the land of Buddhism; there truly are people here who feed monks. Since this is merely a prefecture and county, there is no need to have our travel rescript inspected. Let us beg some food, eat, and then continue our journey.”

p.src: The elder and his three disciples walked slowly along the main street, once again making all the people in the marketplace fearful and suspicious; they crowded around, vying to stare at their appearances. The elder ordered them to keep silent, warning only, “Do not behave wantonly! Do not behave wantonly!” The three duly lowered their heads and dared not look up. Turning a corner, they indeed saw a broad street running north and south.

p.src: As they went on, they saw a gatehouse shaped like a crouching tiger. Inside the gate, a large tablet hung upon the screen wall, bearing the four characters ‘No Monk Among Ten Thousand Shall Be Turned Away.’ Tripitaka said, “This Western land of the Buddha is free of deceit and falsehood among wise and foolish alike. When those two old men spoke of it, I still had my doubts, but now we have arrived and find everything just as they said.” Being a rustic fellow, Eight Rules was about to go straight in. The Pilgrim said, “Stay there, idiot. Wait until someone comes out and we have asked how matters stand; only then should we enter.” Sha Monk said, “Elder Brother is right. If we rush in without distinguishing the inner quarters from the outer, we might annoy our patron.” They set down the horse and luggage at the gate.

p.src: Presently an old servant came out carrying a steelyard and a basket. Catching sight of them without warning, he was so alarmed that he dropped both, fled back inside, and reported, “Master, four extraordinary-looking monks have come outside!” The squire, leaning on his staff, had been strolling idly in the courtyard while ceaselessly reciting the Buddha's name. The moment he heard the report, he cast away his staff and came out to welcome them. On seeing the four pilgrims, he showed no fear of their ugly appearances and merely called, “Please come in! Please come in!” Tripitaka modestly demurred, but they all entered together. After turning down a passage, the squire led them to a building and said, “These rooms on the upper side are the Buddha hall, scripture hall, and refectory where reverend masters such as yourselves are received. Those on the lower side are where my household, old and young, reside.” Tripitaka praised the arrangements without end. He then took out his cassock, put it on, and worshipped the Buddha. Stepping into the hall to look around, he saw:

p.src: When the elder arrived there and was about to bow, the squire again took him by the arm and said, “Please remove your sacred robe.” Tripitaka took off his cassock. Only then did the squire exchange formal greetings with the elder. He also asked the Pilgrim and the other two disciples to exchange greetings with him. He ordered that the horse be fed and the luggage placed beneath the covered walkway, and only then inquired after their welfare. Tripitaka said, “This poor monk is an imperial envoy from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, sent to your honoured region to pay homage at Vulture Peak, behold the Buddha, and seek the true scriptures. Hearing that your household reveres monks, I came to pay my respects and ask for a single vegetarian meal before continuing on my way.” Delight spread across the squire's face, and he said with a beaming smile, “This disciple's humble name is Kou Hong, with the courtesy name Dakuan, and I have idly passed sixty-four years of life. At the age of forty, I vowed to feed ten thousand monks, and only then would my vow be fulfilled. I have now been feeding monks for twenty-four years and keep a ledger of those I have served. Having had little to do these past few days, I counted the names of the monks I had fed. The total was nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-six; I lacked only four holy ones and could not fulfil my vow. Today, by the happiest coincidence, Heaven has sent down you four revered teachers, completing the full number of ten thousand monks. Please leave me your honoured names and, whatever happens, stay at ease for a month or more. Once I have held the ceremony marking the vow's fulfilment, this disciple will provide sedan chairs and horses to convey you revered teachers to the mountain. Vulture Peak is only eight hundred li from here, so the hardship of the road is not great.” Tripitaka was greatly delighted to hear this, and for the time being they all gave their assent; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: His household servants, young and old, went into the residence to carry firewood and water, fetch rice, flour, and vegetables, and prepare the vegetarian offering. This roused the mistress of the house, who asked, “Where have these monks come from, that you are in such a hurry?” The servants replied, “Four holy monks have just arrived. When Master asked after them, one said that they had been sent by the emperor of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha at Vulture Peak. No one knows how far they have traveled to reach us. Master said they had been sent down from Heaven and ordered us to prepare a meal quickly and make offerings to them.” The old woman was delighted to hear this and called to a maid, “Bring me my clothes. I shall go and see them too.” The servant said, “Madam, only one of them is fit to look upon. The other three are dreadful to behold, for they are exceedingly ugly.” The old woman said, “You do not understand. Those whose features are ugly yet strangely distinguished must be celestial beings descended to the mortal world. Hurry and tell your master first.” The servant ran to the scripture hall and told the master, “Madam is coming to pay her respects to the lord from the Eastern Land.” Hearing this, Tripitaka immediately rose from his seat. Before they had finished speaking, the old woman had already reached the hall. She raised her eyes and saw that the Tang Monk had a noble bearing and an imposing, handsome presence. Turning, she saw that Monkey and the other two were extraordinary in appearance. Though she knew they were celestial beings descended to earth, she still felt somewhat terrified and knelt before them. Tripitaka hastily returned her courtesy, saying, “You trouble yourself, good bodhisattva, by showing us such undeserved respect.” The old woman asked the master, “Why are the four reverend monks not seated together?” Pursing his snout, Bajie said, “The three of us are disciples.” “Eh!” His cry sounded like a tiger roaring in the deep mountains, and frightened the old lady all the more.

p.src: While they were speaking, another servant came to report, “The two young masters have arrived as well.” Tripitaka quickly turned to look and saw two young scholars. The two scholars entered the scripture hall and prostrated themselves before the elder. Startled, Tripitaka hurriedly returned their bows. The master stepped forward and caught hold of them, saying, “These are my two younger sons, named Kou Liang and Kou Dong. They have just returned from their studies to eat their midday meal. When they learned that you had descended to our home, Master, they came to pay their respects.” Tripitaka said with delight, “Excellent, excellent! As the saying goes: ‘To raise the standing of your house, you must do good; to have worthy descendants, see that they study.’” The two scholars asked their father, “Where has this venerable lord come from?” The master laughed. “From very far away. He is an imperial envoy sent by the emperor of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land of Southern Jambudvipa, going to Vulture Peak to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures.” One scholar said, “I read in the Comprehensive Record of the Forest of Affairs that there are but four great continents beneath Heaven. Our land is called Western Cattle-Gift Continent, and there is also an Eastern Pūrvavideha Continent. Coming here from Southern Jambudvipa must have taken you no one knows how many years?” Tripitaka smiled. “During my journey, the days of delay have been many and the days of travel few. Again and again we have met vicious demons and savage monsters and endured untold hardships. I owe a great debt to my three disciples for protecting me. Fourteen winters and summers have passed in all before we reached this blessed region.” On hearing this, the scholars praised him without cease: “A truly divine monk! A truly divine monk!”

p.src: Look at them: some brought soup while others added rice, hurrying back and forth like shooting stars chasing the moon. Zhu Bajie swallowed a bowl at a mouthful, sweeping the dishes away like a gale scattering the last clouds. Master and disciples thoroughly enjoyed the meal. The elder rose, thanked the master for the meal, and made ready to continue his journey. The master stopped him, saying, “Please set your mind at ease and stay a few days, Master. As the saying goes, ‘It is easy to begin, but hard to bring a thing to completion.’ Only when I have held the final rite may I presume to see you on your way.” Seeing his sincere and earnest heart, Tripitaka had no choice but to stay.

p.src: Thus they continued for three days and nights, and the service was completed. The Tang Monk thought of Thunderclap Monastery and longed wholeheartedly to press on, so once more he offered his thanks and farewells. The master said, “You are so eager to depart, Master. Can it be that the bustle of these past days’ services made me neglect you, and you have taken offense?” Tripitaka replied, “We have imposed deeply upon your honored household, and I know not how to repay you. How could I possibly take offense? It is only that when the holy sovereign saw me beyond the frontier and asked when I might return, I rashly answered that I would be back in three years. Unexpected delays on the road, however, have now made it fourteen years. I do not yet know whether we shall obtain the scriptures, and the return journey will take another twelve or thirteen years. Would that not defy the imperial command? How could I bear the guilt? I beg you, venerable sir, to let this poor monk proceed. Once we have obtained the scriptures and are on our way back, why should we not visit your residence again and stay somewhat longer?”

p.src: Unable to contain himself, Bajie cried aloud, “Master, you are far too unwilling to grant another’s wishes and utterly unreasonable. This venerable master is a wealthy lord of a great household. He vowed to feed monks so lavishly, and now his vow is fulfilled; moreover, he is asking us to stay with perfect sincerity. Remaining for a year or so would do no harm, so why insist on leaving? You would abandon such fine ready-prepared food only to go begging at other people’s doors. Have you some honored father or mother waiting for you farther down the road?” The elder shouted sharply, “You oaf! You care only for good food and pay no heed to the purpose of dedicating merit. You are nothing but a beast that feeds at the trough and scratches an itch inside its belly. Since you all choose to cling to greed, anger, and delusion here, tomorrow I shall go on alone.” Seeing his master’s face darken, Monkey seized Bajie and pummeled him about the head, cursing, “You idiot! You do not know what is good for you. You have made Master angry with all of us.” Sha Monk laughed. “Well hit, well hit! Even when you keep quiet you are an annoyance, yet you still have to interrupt.” The idiot stood fuming at one side and dared not say another word. Seeing discord arise among master and disciples, the host could only force a broad smile and say, “Please do not be vexed, Master. Be a little forbearing for today. Tomorrow I shall prepare banners and drums and invite some neighbors and relatives to see you set forth.”

p.src: While they were speaking, the old lady came out again and said, “Reverend Father, since you have honored our humble home, you need not insist on declining. How many days have you been here now?” Tripitaka replied, “Half a month already.” The old lady said, “Count this first half-month as my husband’s meritorious offering. I too have a little money saved from my needlework, and I wish to provide you reverend fathers with meals for another half-month.” Before she had finished, the brothers Kou Dong came out and said, “My lords, our father has fed monks for over twenty years, yet never before has he met such worthy men. Now, just as his vow is fulfilled, you four have graciously descended upon us; truly, your presence has brought glory to our humble dwelling. We are young and understand little of karmic reward, but we often hear it said, ‘What the husband cultivates, the husband gains; what the wife cultivates, the wife gains; one who cultivates nothing gains nothing.’ Our father and mother each wish to offer their humble fare precisely so that each may reap some karmic reward. Why must you insist on refusing? Even we foolish brothers have saved a little from our tutors’ fees and hope to support you for half a month before seeing you on your way.” Tripitaka said, “I dare not even accept your honored mother’s generous kindness; how then could I presume upon the great affection of you worthy brothers? I most certainly cannot accept. We are resolved to depart this morning; please do not take offense. Otherwise, having long exceeded the imperial deadline, I would incur a crime worthy of death.” When the old lady and her two sons saw that his determination could not be shaken, they grew annoyed and said, “We kindly ask him to stay, yet he is so obstinately bent on leaving. If he wishes to go, let him go. What is the use of all this endless talk?” Mother and sons then withdrew inside.

p.src: Unable to hold his tongue, Bajie said to the Tang Monk again, “Master, do not carry things too far. As the saying goes, ‘Refuse to stay, and you will only invite resentment.’ Let us stay for a month and fulfill the wishes of the mother and her sons. Why must we be in such a hurry?” The Tang Monk barked another rebuke. The fool slapped his own mouth twice and said, “Pah, pah, pah! I told myself not to talk too much, yet I have opened my mouth again!” Wukong and Sha Monk snickered together off to one side. The Tang Monk then turned on Wukong and said, “What are you laughing at?” He immediately formed the hand sign, ready to recite the Tight-Fillet Spell. Wukong was so alarmed that he dropped to his knees and said, “Master, I was not laughing, I was not laughing. Please, whatever you do, do not recite it! Do not recite it!”

Please, whatever you do, do not recite it! Do not recite it!”

p.src: When the squire saw discord gradually arising among master and disciples, he no longer dared press them to stay and merely said, “Reverend Fathers, there is no need to quarrel. I agree to see you off tomorrow morning.” He left the scripture hall and ordered his clerks to write over a hundred invitation cards, summoning neighbors and relatives to see the reverend fathers from the Tang court off on their westward journey the next morning. At the same time he ordered the cooks to prepare a farewell banquet; and he ordered the stewards to make twenty pairs of colored banners, engage a band of wind and percussion musicians, invite a company of monks from the temple to the south and a company of Daoist priests from the Temple of the Eastern Peak, all of whom were to be fully assembled by the hour of the Snake the next day. The attendants received their orders and departed.

p.src: During the third and fourth watches that night, the household servants under the various stewards all rose early to purchase the many things required. Look at those arranging the banquet, bustling frantically in the kitchen; those setting out the colored banners, clamoring before the hall; those inviting monks and Daoists, running their legs off; those summoning the musicians, hurrying with their whole bodies; those delivering invitations, racing east and west; and those preparing sedan chairs and horses, calling and answering from above and below. The clamor continued from midnight until dawn. Around the hour of the Snake everything was ready—such things are easily done when one has money.

p.src: Now the Tang Monk and his disciples rose early and were once again served by a company of attendants. The elder ordered them to pack the luggage and saddle the horse. When the fool heard they were leaving, he thrust out his mouth and thick lips and muttered under his breath; but he had no choice except to pack the robes and alms bowl and bring out the high-shouldered carrying pole. Sha Monk brushed and washed the horse, saddled and bridled it, and stood waiting. Wukong handed the nine-ringed staff to his master and hung the pouch containing their travel document around his own chest; they were all ready to depart. The squire invited them all to the great rear hall, where another banquet had been laid out, far grander than the meals with which they had been entertained in the refectory. And this is what could be seen:

p.src: As the elder was exchanging courtesies with the squire, a house servant came to report, “The guests have all arrived.” They were the invited neighbors from both sides, brothers-in-law of every relation, together with fellow lay devotees who provided monastic meals and pious friends who recited the Buddha’s name; all bowed to the elder in unison. When the bows were finished, each took his assigned seat. Below the hall, zithers sounded and reed pipes played; within the hall, strings and songs accompanied the feast and wine. Bajie fixed his attention on this sumptuous feast and said to Sha Monk, “Brother, open your heart and stretch your capacity—eat as much as you can. Once we leave the Kou household, we shall never find such rich fare again.” Sha Monk laughed and said, “Second Brother, what are you saying? As the proverb goes, ‘Of a hundred delicacies and flavors, one full meal is enough.’ One may have private provisions for the road, but who has a private stomach to store them in?” Bajie said, “You are truly hopeless, utterly hopeless. If I eat my absolute fill at this meal, I will not be in any hurry to feel hungry even after three days.” Hearing this, Wukong said, “Fool, do not burst your belly. We have a journey to make now.”

p.src: Before long, the sun approached noon. The elder, seated at the head, raised his chopsticks and recited the Sutra for Concluding the Meal. Bajie panicked, seized the rice bowl as it was brought for refilling, and gulped down one bowl at a mouthful, disposing of five or six bowls more. Then he indiscriminately stuffed steamed buns, filled pastries, flat cakes, and baked fruit until both sleeves bulged, and only then rose to follow his master. The elder thanked the squire, then thanked all the guests, and they went out together. Outside the gate stood colored banners, jeweled canopies, drummers, and musicians; the two companies of monks and Daoists had also just arrived. The squire laughed and said, “You gentlemen have come late, while the reverend fathers are in haste to leave. There is no time to offer you a meal, so I shall thank you properly when I return.” Everyone cleared the road. Those with sedan chairs shouldered them, those with horses mounted, and those on foot walked, all yielding the lead to the elder and his three disciples. Music thundered to the heavens, banners blotted out the sun, crowds thronged together, and carriages and horses packed the road; everyone had come to watch Squire Kou escort the Tang Monk on his departure. The splendor of the occasion truly surpassed a gathering wreathed in pearls and kingfisher feathers and was in no way inferior to springtime concealed within brocade curtains. The company of monks played a suite of Buddhist music; and the company of Daoists performed a strain of mystic music. They all escorted the travelers beyond the prefectural city to the ten-li pavilion, where baskets of food and jars of drink had again been laid out. Raising cups and offering goblets, they drank together and bade farewell. Still unable to bear parting, the squire said with tears in his eyes, “Reverend Father, when you return after obtaining the scriptures, you must come to my home and stay a few more days, so that the wish of this Kou Hong may be fulfilled.” Tripitaka was endlessly moved and thanked him again and again, saying, “If I reach Vulture Peak and behold the Buddha, I shall first declare your great virtue to him. On my return, I shall certainly come to your door and offer my thanks in person.” As they talked, they unknowingly went another two or three li. The elder then earnestly bowed and took his leave. The squire burst into loud sobs once more before turning back. Indeed:

p.src: We shall say no more of how Squire Kou escorted them as far as the pavilion ten li away before returning home with the others. Now the four pilgrims, master and disciples, had traveled some forty or fifty li when evening began to fall. The elder said, “Night is falling. Where shall we find lodging?” Bajie, carrying the luggage and thrusting out his lips, said, “We left ready-cooked food uneaten and cool tiled rooms unused, only to hurry along as though racing to a funeral or chasing after a wandering soul. Now that night has come, what are we to do if it starts raining?” Sanzang scolded him: “You wretched beast! Complaining again, are you? As the saying goes, ‘Though Chang’an is a fine place, it is no home in which to linger forever.’ When destiny permits us to worship the Buddha and obtain the true scriptures, we shall return to the Great Tang and report to our sovereign. Then you may eat the food from the imperial kitchens for years on end, until you burst, you brute, and become a ghost with a full belly.” The fool chuckled secretly to himself and dared say no more.

p.src: Wukong raised his eyes and looked into the distance. Seeing several buildings beside the main road, he hastily called to his master, “We can rest there! We can rest there!” When the elder drew near, he saw a ruined ceremonial archway. An old plaque hung upon it, bearing four large characters whose color had faded beneath accumulated dust: “Huaguang Lodge.” The elder dismounted and said, “Bodhisattva Huaguang was a disciple of the Buddha of Fivefold Fiery Radiance. Because he destroyed the Venomous Fire Demon King, he was demoted and transformed into the Five Manifestations Numinous Official. There must surely be a temple keeper here.” They all went inside, only to find that every room along the galleries had collapsed and not a person was in sight. They were about to withdraw when, unexpectedly, black clouds covered the sky and rain came pouring down. With no other choice, they found a place beneath the ruined buildings that afforded some shelter from wind and rain and took refuge there. They remained utterly quiet, not daring to raise their voices for fear that some demon or evil spirit might notice them. Some sat and others stood, enduring the whole night in misery without sleep. Ah! Truly it was this:
